• [Way forward] Fund indigenous neuroscience research with ethical oversight and translational pathways.
• [Conclusion] An algal protein became a tool for brain circuits, underscoring the case for funding curiosity-driven research alongside translational targets.

CA Topic / Headline: Drishti IAS (fallback 05-10): Delhi High Court held that a valid Indian visa does not guarantee entry, as immigration officers at ports of entry decide; a Turkmenistan citizen with a valid business visa was denied entry on adverse intelligence; the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025 governs entry.
Prelims Recall (CSE 2027):
• A valid visa is conditional authorisation; the final entry decision rests with immigration officers at ports of entry.
• Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025: Section 3 requires a valid passport or visa; Section 7 lets the Centre prohibit, regulate or restrict entry.
• Foreigners hold Article 21 rights; Article 19(1)(e) residence rights are exclusive to citizens.
• Hans Muller of Nurenburg v. Superintendent (1955) and Louis De Raedt v. Union (1991) treat entry and exit as sovereign functions.
Mains Recall (CSE 2027):
• [Judgment] Delhi High Court: entry is a sovereign function with absolute discretion; officers can refuse entry despite a valid visa.
• [Issue] Adverse intelligence can bar entry, but refusal without disclosed reasons raises natural-justice concerns.
• [Counterpoint] Foreigners hold only Article 21 protection, so sovereign discretion outweighs expectations created by a visa.
• [Way forward] Record reasons for refusal in sensitive cases and provide a review channel while preserving security discretion.
• [Conclusion] The ruling aligns India with the sovereign-discretion norm in immigration law; accountability must come from reasoned records, not a right to enter.
